Minerals and Energy Resources

From a pin to a ship, everything we use is made from minerals — and everything that moves runs on energy. This chapter maps the occurrence, distribution and conservation of India’s minerals, then works through conventional and non-conventional sources of energy.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

We use different things in our daily life made from metal. The earth’s crust is made up of different minerals embedded in the rocks, and various metals are extracted from these minerals after proper refinement. Minerals are an indispensable part of our lives: almost everything we use, from a tiny pin to a towering building or a big ship, is made from minerals — railway lines, the tarmac of roads, implements and machinery, cars, buses, trains and aeroplanes, and even the food we eat.

The chapter begins with what a mineral is and how geographers and geologists study it differently, then explains the modes of occurrence of minerals: in igneous and metamorphic rocks as veins and lodes, in sedimentary rocks as beds and layers, as residual masses after decomposition, as placer deposits in valley floors, and in ocean waters and beds.

It then describes the distribution of India’s minerals — ferrous (iron ore, manganese), non-ferrous (copper, bauxite), non-metallic (mica) and rock minerals (limestone) — along with the hazards of mining and the need for conservation.

The last part covers energy resources: conventional sources (firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas, electricity) and non-conventional sources (nuclear, solar, wind, biogas, tidal, geothermal), and ends with the principle that “energy saved is energy produced”.

Mineral

A homogenous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure; over 2,000 minerals have been identified.

Ore

An accumulation of any mineral mixed with other elements, in sufficient concentration to make extraction commercially viable.

Veins and lodes

Smaller and larger occurrences of minerals in cracks, crevices, faults or joints of igneous and metamorphic rocks.

Placer deposits

Alluvial deposits in the sands of valley floors and the base of hills, containing minerals not corroded by water — gold, silver, tin, platinum.

Iron ore

Magnetite (up to 70% iron) and hematite (50–60%); in 2018–19, 97% of production came from Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Jharkhand.

Bauxite

Odisha was the largest producer in 2018–19 (65%); Panchpatmali deposits in Koraput district are the most important.

Coal

Peat, lignite (Neyveli), bituminous and anthracite; Gondwana coal in the Damodar valley and tertiary coal in the north-east.

Energy

Conventional and non-conventional; over 70 per cent of rural household energy comes from firewood and cattle dung cake.

Minerals in Our Lives

We use different things in our daily life made from metal. The earth’s crust is made up of different minerals embedded in the rocks. Various metals are extracted from these minerals after proper refinement.

Minerals are an indispensable part of our lives. Almost everything we use, from a tiny pin to a towering building or a big ship, all are made from minerals. The railway lines and the tarmac (paving) of the roads, our implements and machinery too are made from minerals. Cars, buses, trains, aeroplanes are manufactured from minerals and run on power resources derived from the earth. Even the food that we eat contains minerals. In all stages of development, human beings have used minerals for their livelihood, decoration, festivities, religious and ceremonial rites.

Chapter story

Haban comes to Guwahati with his father from a remote village. He sees people getting into strange house-like objects which move along the road. He also sees a “kitchen” dragging a number of houses along with it. He is amazed and asks his father, “Why don’t our houses move like the one we saw in Guwahati, Ba?” His father replies, “These are not houses, they are buses and trains. Unlike our houses these are not made of bricks and stones; metal like iron and aluminium are used in making these. They do not move on their own. They are driven by an engine which needs energy to work.”

Box: minerals in toothpaste

A bright smile from toothpaste and minerals: toothpaste cleans your teeth. Abrasive minerals like silica, limestone, aluminium oxide and various phosphate minerals do the cleaning. Fluoride, which is used to reduce cavities, comes from a mineral fluorite. Most toothpaste is made white with titanium oxide, which comes from minerals called rutile, ilmenite and anatase. The sparkle in some toothpastes comes from mica. The toothbrush and the tube containing the paste are made of plastics from petroleum.

All living things need minerals. Life processes cannot occur without minerals. Although our mineral intake represents only about 0.3 per cent of our total intake of nutrients, they are so potent and so important that without them we would not be able to utilise the other 99.7 per cent of foodstuffs.

Activities

Find out where these minerals are found. Dig a little deeper and find out how many minerals are used to make a light bulb. Collect “Nutritional Facts” printed on food labels.

What is a Mineral?
NCERT definition

Geologists define a mineral as a “homogenous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure.” Minerals are found in varied forms in nature, ranging from the hardest diamond to the softest talc.

Rocks are combinations of homogenous substances called minerals. Some rocks, for instance limestone, consist of a single mineral only, but the majority of rocks consist of several minerals in varying proportions. Although over 2,000 minerals have been identified, only a few are abundantly found in most of the rocks.

A particular mineral that will be formed from a certain combination of elements depends upon the physical and chemical conditions under which the material forms. This, in turn, results in a wide range of colours, hardness, crystal forms, lustre and density that a particular mineral possesses. Geologists use these properties to classify the minerals.

Study of minerals by geographers and geologists
GeographerGeologist
Studies minerals as part of the earth’s crust for a better understanding of landforms; interested in the distribution of mineral resources and associated economic activities.Interested in the formation of minerals, their age, and physical and chemical composition.

However, for general and commercial purposes, minerals can be classified as under:

Mode of Occurrence of Minerals

Minerals are usually found in “ores”. The term ore is used to describe an accumulation of any mineral mixed with other elements. The mineral content of the ore must be in sufficient concentration to make its extraction commercially viable. The type of formation or structure in which they are found determines the relative ease with which mineral ores may be mined, and this also determines the cost of extraction.

Minerals generally occur in these forms:

  1. In igneous and metamorphic rocks, minerals may occur in the cracks, crevices, faults or joints. The smaller occurrences are called veins and the larger are called lodes. In most cases they are formed when minerals in liquid/molten and gaseous forms are forced upward through cavities towards the earth’s surface; they cool and solidify as they rise. Major metallic minerals like tin, copper, zinc and lead are obtained from veins and lodes.
  2. In sedimentary rocks, a number of minerals occur in beds or layers. They have been formed as a result of deposition, accumulation and concentration in horizontal strata. Coal and some forms of iron ore have been concentrated as a result of long periods under great heat and pressure. Another group of sedimentary minerals includes gypsum, potash salt and sodium salt, formed as a result of evaporation, especially in arid regions.
  3. Another mode of formation involves the decomposition of surface rocks and the removal of soluble constituents, leaving a residual mass of weathered material containing ores. Bauxite is formed this way.
  4. Certain minerals may occur as alluvial deposits in the sands of valley floors and the base of hills. These deposits are called “placer deposits” and generally contain minerals which are not corroded by water. Gold, silver, tin and platinum are most important among such minerals.
  5. The ocean waters contain vast quantities of minerals, but most of these are too widely diffused to be of economic significance. However, common salt, magnesium and bromine are largely derived from ocean waters. The ocean beds, too, are rich in manganese nodules.
Box: Rat-hole mining

Rat-Hole Mining: most of the minerals in India are nationalised and their extraction is possible only after obtaining due permission from the government. But in most of the tribal areas of north-east India, minerals are owned by individuals or communities. In Meghalaya there are large deposits of coal, iron ore, limestone and dolomite. Coal mining in Jowai and Cherapunjee is done by family members in the form of a long narrow tunnel, known as “rat-hole” mining. The National Green Tribunal has declared such activities illegal and recommended that these should be stopped forthwith.

Distribution of Minerals in India

India is fortunate to have fairly rich and varied mineral resources. However, these are unevenly distributed.

  • Broadly speaking, peninsular rocks contain most of the reserves of coal, metallic minerals, mica and many other non-metallic minerals.
  • Sedimentary rocks on the western and eastern flanks of the peninsula, in Gujarat and Assam, have most of the petroleum deposits.
  • Rajasthan, with the rock systems of the peninsula, has reserves of many non-ferrous minerals.
  • The vast alluvial plains of north India are almost devoid of economic minerals.

These variations exist largely because of the differences in the geological structure, processes and time involved in the formation of minerals.

Always remember that the concentration of mineral in the ore, the ease of extraction and closeness to the market play an important role in affecting the economic viability of a reserve. Thus, to meet the demand, a choice has to be made between a number of possible options. When this is done, a mineral “deposit” or “reserve” turns into a mine.

Ferrous Minerals: Iron Ore and Manganese

Ferrous minerals account for about three-fourths of the total value of the production of metallic minerals. They provide a strong base for the development of metallurgical industries. India exports substantial quantities of ferrous minerals after meeting her internal demands.

Iron ore

Iron ore is the basic mineral and the backbone of industrial development. India is endowed with fairly abundant resources of iron ore and is rich in good quality iron ores.

Types of iron ore
TypeIron contentSpecial quality
MagnetiteUp to 70 per centThe finest iron ore, with excellent magnetic qualities, especially valuable in the electrical industry
Hematite50–60 per centThe most important industrial iron ore in terms of the quantity used, but with a slightly lower iron content than magnetite

In 2018–19 almost the entire production of iron ore (97%) accrued from Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Jharkhand. The remaining production (3%) was from other states.

The major iron ore belts in India are:

  • Odisha–Jharkhand belt: in Odisha, high grade hematite ore is found in Badampahar mines in the Mayurbhanj and Kendujhar districts. In the adjoining Singbhum district of Jharkhand, haematite iron ore is mined in Gua and Noamundi.
  • Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur belt lies in Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra. Very high grade hematites are found in the famous Bailadila range of hills in the Bastar district of Chhattisgarh. The range comprises 14 deposits of super high grade hematite iron ore, and has the best physical properties needed for steel making. Iron ore from these mines is exported to Japan and South Korea via Vishakhapatnam port.
  • Ballari–Chitradurga–Chikkamagaluru–Tumakuru belt in Karnataka has large reserves of iron ore. The Kudremukh mines located in the Western Ghats of Karnataka are a 100 per cent export unit. Kudremukh deposits are known to be one of the largest in the world. The ore is transported as slurry through a pipeline to a port near Mangaluru.
  • Maharashtra–Goa belt includes the state of Goa and Ratnagiri district of Maharashtra. Though the ores are not of very high quality, they are efficiently exploited. Iron ore is exported through Marmagao port.
Box: how places got their names

Kudre in Kannada means horse. The highest peak in the Western Ghats of Karnataka resembles the face of a horse. The Bailadila hills look like the hump of an ox, and hence its name.

Manganese

Manganese is mainly used in the manufacturing of steel and ferro-manganese alloy. Nearly 10 kg of manganese is required to manufacture one tonne of steel. It is also used in manufacturing bleaching powder, insecticides and paints.

Non-Ferrous Minerals: Copper and Bauxite

India’s reserves and production of non-ferrous minerals is not very satisfactory. However, these minerals, which include copper, bauxite, lead, zinc and gold, play a vital role in a number of metallurgical, engineering and electrical industries.

Copper

India is critically deficient in the reserve and production of copper. Being malleable, ductile and a good conductor, copper is mainly used in electrical cables, electronics and chemical industries. The Balaghat mines in Madhya Pradesh, Khetri mines in Rajasthan and Singhbhum district of Jharkhand are leading producers of copper.

Bauxite

Though several ores contain aluminium, it is from bauxite, a clay-like substance, that alumina and later aluminium is obtained. Bauxite deposits are formed by the decomposition of a wide variety of rocks rich in aluminium silicates.

Aluminium is an important metal because it combines the strength of metals such as iron with extreme lightness, and also with good conductivity and great malleability. India’s bauxite deposits are mainly found in the Amarkantak plateau, Maikal hills and the plateau region of Bilaspur–Katni.

Odisha was the largest bauxite producing state in India in 2018–19. Panchpatmali deposits in Koraput district are the most important bauxite deposits in the state.

Box: the value of aluminium

After the discovery of aluminium: Emperor Napoleon III wore buttons and hooks on his clothes made of aluminium and served food to his more illustrious guests in aluminium utensils, while the less honourable ones were served in gold and silver utensils. Thirty years after this incident, aluminium bowls were most common with the beggars in Paris.

Non-Metallic Minerals: Mica, and Rock Minerals: Limestone

Mica

Mica is a mineral made up of a series of plates or leaves. It splits easily into thin sheets — so thin that a thousand can be layered into a mica sheet a few centimetres high. Mica can be clear, black, green, red, yellow or brown.

Due to its excellent di-electric strength, low power loss factor, insulating properties and resistance to high voltage, mica is one of the most indispensable minerals used in electric and electronic industries.

Mica deposits are found in the northern edge of the Chota Nagpur plateau. The Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand is the leading producer. In Rajasthan the major mica producing area is around Ajmer. The Nellore mica belt of Andhra Pradesh is also an important producer.

Rock minerals — limestone

Limestone is found in association with rocks composed of calcium carbonates or calcium and magnesium carbonates. It is found in sedimentary rocks of most geological formations. Limestone is the basic raw material for the cement industry and essential for smelting iron ore in the blast furnace.

Hazards of Mining and Conservation of Minerals

Have you ever wondered about the efforts miners make in making life comfortable for you? What are the impacts of mining on the health of the miners and the environment?

  • The dust and noxious fumes inhaled by miners make them vulnerable to pulmonary diseases.
  • The risk of collapsing mine roofs, inundation and fires in coalmines is a constant threat to miners.
  • The water sources in the region get contaminated due to mining.
  • Dumping of waste and slurry leads to degradation of land, soil, and increase in stream and river pollution.

Stricter safety regulations and implementation of environmental laws are essential to prevent mining from becoming a “killer industry”.

Conservation of minerals

We all appreciate the strong dependence of industry and agriculture upon mineral deposits and the substances manufactured from them. The total volume of workable mineral deposits is an insignificant fraction — one per cent — of the earth’s crust. We are rapidly consuming mineral resources that required millions of years to be created and concentrated. The geological processes of mineral formation are so slow that the rates of replenishment are infinitely small in comparison to the present rates of consumption.

Mineral resources are therefore finite and non-renewable. Rich mineral deposits are our country’s extremely valuable but short-lived possessions. Continued extraction of ores leads to increasing costs as mineral extraction comes from greater depths along with a decrease in quality.

A concerted effort has to be made in order to use our mineral resources in a planned and sustainable manner. Improved technologies need to be constantly evolved to allow use of low grade ores at low costs. Recycling of metals, using scrap metals and other substitutes are steps in conserving our mineral resources for the future.

Energy Resources: An Introduction

Energy is required for all activities. It is needed to cook, to provide light and heat, to propel vehicles and to drive machinery in industries. Energy can be generated from fuel minerals like coal, petroleum, natural gas and uranium, and from electricity.

Classification of energy resources
Conventional sourcesNon-conventional sources
Firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity (both hydel and thermal)Solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and atomic energy

Firewood and cattle dung cake are most common in rural India. According to one estimate, more than 70 per cent of the energy requirement in rural households is met by these two; continuation of these is increasingly becoming difficult due to the decreasing forest area. Moreover, using dung cake is being discouraged because it consumes the most valuable manure which could be used in agriculture.

Conventional Sources of Energy

Coal

In India, coal is the most abundantly available fossil fuel. It provides a substantial part of the nation’s energy needs. It is used for power generation, to supply energy to industry as well as for domestic needs. India is highly dependent on coal for meeting its commercial energy requirements.

Coal is formed due to the compression of plant material over millions of years. Coal is therefore found in a variety of forms depending on the degrees of compression and the depth and time of burial.

Forms of coal
FormDescription
PeatProduced by decaying plants in swamps; low carbon and high moisture content, and low heating capacity
LigniteA low grade brown coal, soft with high moisture content; the principal lignite reserves are in Neyveli in Tamil Nadu, used for generation of electricity
Bituminous coalCoal buried deep and subjected to increased temperatures; the most popular coal in commercial use
AnthraciteThe highest quality hard coal
Metallurgical coalHigh grade bituminous coal with a special value for smelting iron in blast furnaces

In India, coal occurs in rock series of two main geological ages: Gondwana, a little over 200 million years in age, and tertiary deposits which are only about 55 million years old. The major resources of Gondwana coal, which are metallurgical coal, are located in the Damodar valley (West Bengal–Jharkhand). Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro are important coalfields. The Godavari, Mahanadi, Son and Wardha valleys also contain coal deposits. Tertiary coals occur in the north-eastern states of Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland.

Remember, coal is a bulky material which loses weight on use as it is reduced to ash. Hence heavy industries and thermal power stations are located on or near the coalfields.

Petroleum

Petroleum or mineral oil is the next major energy source in India after coal. It provides fuel for heat and lighting, lubricants for machinery and raw materials for a number of manufacturing industries. Petroleum refineries act as a “nodal industry” for synthetic textile, fertiliser and numerous chemical industries.

Most of the petroleum occurrences in India are associated with anticlines and fault traps in the rock formations of the tertiary age. In regions of folding, anticlines or domes, oil occurs where oil is trapped in the crest of the upfold. The oil-bearing layer is a porous limestone or sandstone through which oil may flow; the oil is prevented from rising or sinking by intervening non-porous layers. Petroleum is also found in fault traps between porous and non-porous rocks. Gas, being lighter, usually occurs above the oil.

Mumbai High, Gujarat and Assam are major petroleum production areas in India. Ankeleshwar is the most important field of Gujarat. Assam is the oldest oil producing state of India, with Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran-Hugrijan as important oil fields.

Natural gas

Natural gas is found with petroleum deposits and is released when crude oil is brought to the surface. It can be used as a domestic and industrial fuel. It is used as fuel in the power sector to generate electricity, for heating purposes in industries, as raw material in chemical, petrochemical and fertiliser industries, as transport fuel and as cooking fuel. With the expansion of gas infrastructure and local city gas distribution networks, natural gas is emerging as a preferred transport fuel (CNG) and cooking fuel (PNG) at homes.

India’s major gas reserves are found in the Mumbai High and allied fields along the west coast, supplemented by finds in the Cambay basin. Along the east coast, new reserves of natural gas have been discovered in the Krishna–Godavari basin.

The first 1,700 km long Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur (HVJ) cross-country gas pipeline, constructed by GAIL (India), linked Mumbai High and Bassein gas fields with various fertiliser, power and industrial complexes in western and northern India. This artery provided impetus to Indian gas market development. Overall, India’s gas infrastructure has expanded over ten times from 1,700 km to 18,500 km of cross-country pipelines and is expected to soon reach over 34,000 km as a Gas Grid by linking all gas sources and consuming markets across the country, including the North-Eastern states.

Activity

Collect information about cross-country natural gas pipelines laid by GAIL (India) under “One Nation One Grid”.

Electricity

Electricity has such a wide range of applications in today’s world that its per capita consumption is considered as an index of development. Electricity is generated mainly in two ways: by running water, which drives hydro turbines to generate hydro electricity; and by burning other fuels such as coal, petroleum and natural gas to drive turbines to produce thermal power. Once generated, the electricity is exactly the same.

  • Hydro electricity is generated by fast flowing water, which is a renewable resource. India has a number of multi-purpose projects like the Bhakra Nangal, Damodar Valley Corporation and the Kopili Hydel Project, producing hydroelectric power.
  • Thermal electricity is generated by using coal, petroleum and natural gas. Thermal power stations use non-renewable fossil fuels for generating electricity.
Activities

Name some river valley projects and write the names of the dams built on these rivers. Collect information about thermal/hydel power plants located in your state and show them on the map of India.

Non-Conventional Sources of Energy

The growing consumption of energy has resulted in the country becoming increasingly dependent on fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. Rising prices of oil and gas and their potential shortages have raised uncertainties about the security of energy supply in future, which in turn has serious repercussions on the growth of the national economy. Moreover, increasing use of fossil fuels also causes serious environmental problems. Hence there is a pressing need to use renewable energy sources like solar energy, wind, tide, biomass and energy from waste material. These are called non-conventional energy sources. India is blessed with an abundance of sunlight, water, wind and biomass, and has the largest programmes for the development of these renewable energy resources.

Nuclear or atomic energy

It is obtained by altering the structure of atoms. When such an alteration is made, much energy is released in the form of heat, and this is used to generate electric power. Uranium and thorium, which are available in Jharkhand and the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan, are used for generating atomic or nuclear power. The monazite sands of Kerala are also rich in thorium.

Activity

Locate the 6 nuclear power stations and find out the state in which they are located.

Solar energy

India is a tropical country. It has enormous possibilities of tapping solar energy. Photovoltaic technology converts sunlight directly into electricity. Solar energy is fast becoming popular in rural and remote areas. Some big solar power plants are being established in different parts of India, which will minimise the dependence of rural households on firewood and dung cakes, and in turn contribute to environmental conservation and adequate supply of manure in agriculture.

Wind power

India has great potential of wind power. The largest wind farm cluster is located in Tamil Nadu from Nagarcoil to Madurai. Apart from these, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Gujarat, Kerala, Maharashtra and Lakshadweep have important wind farms. Nagarcoil and Jaisalmer are well known for effective use of wind energy in the country.

Biogas

Shrubs, farm waste, animal and human waste are used to produce biogas for domestic consumption in rural areas. Decomposition of organic matter yields gas, which has higher thermal efficiency in comparison to kerosene, dung cake and charcoal. Biogas plants are set up at municipal, cooperative and individual levels. The plants using cattle dung are known as “gobar gas plants” in rural India. These provide twin benefits to the farmer in the form of energy and improved quality of manure. Biogas is by far the most efficient use of cattle dung: it improves the quality of manure and also prevents the loss of trees and manure due to burning of fuel wood and cow dung cakes.

Tidal energy

Oceanic tides can be used to generate electricity. Floodgate dams are built across inlets. During high tide water flows into the inlet and gets trapped when the gate is closed. After the tide falls outside the flood gate, the water retained by the floodgate flows back to the sea via a pipe that carries it through a power-generating turbine. In India, the Gulf of Khambhat, the Gulf of Kuchchh in Gujarat on the western coast and the Gangetic delta in the Sunderban regions of West Bengal provide ideal conditions for utilising tidal energy.

Geo thermal energy

Geo thermal energy refers to the heat and electricity produced by using the heat from the interior of the Earth. Geothermal energy exists because the earth grows progressively hotter with increasing depth. Where the geothermal gradient is high, high temperatures are found at shallow depths. Groundwater in such areas absorbs heat from the rocks and becomes hot; it is so hot that when it rises to the earth’s surface it turns into steam, which is used to drive turbines and generate electricity.

There are several hundred hot springs in India which could be used to generate electricity. Two experimental projects have been set up in India to harness geothermal energy: one in the Parvati valley near Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh, and the other in the Puga Valley, Ladakh.

Conservation of Energy Resources

Energy is a basic requirement for economic development. Every sector of the national economy — agriculture, industry, transport, commercial and domestic — needs inputs of energy. The economic development plans implemented since Independence necessarily required increasing amounts of energy to remain operational. As a result, consumption of energy in all forms has been steadily rising all over the country.

In this background, there is an urgent need to develop a sustainable path of energy development. Promotion of energy conservation and increased use of renewable energy sources are the twin planks of sustainable energy.

India is presently one of the least energy efficient countries in the world. We have to adopt a cautious approach for the judicious use of our limited energy resources. As concerned citizens we can do our bit by using public transport systems instead of individual vehicles, switching off electricity when not in use, using power-saving devices and using non-conventional sources of energy. After all, “energy saved is energy produced”.

All key terms

Key terms and definitions
TermSimple explanation
MineralA homogenous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure; geologists classify minerals by colour, hardness, crystal form, lustre and density.
OreAn accumulation of any mineral mixed with other elements, in sufficient concentration to make extraction commercially viable.
VeinA smaller occurrence of minerals in cracks, crevices, faults or joints of igneous and metamorphic rocks.
LodeA larger occurrence of minerals in cracks, crevices, faults or joints; tin, copper, zinc and lead come from veins and lodes.
Placer depositAn alluvial deposit in the sands of valley floors and the base of hills, containing minerals not corroded by water — gold, silver, tin, platinum.
Manganese noduleA mineral-rich nodule found on ocean beds.
Rat-hole miningCoal mining through a long narrow tunnel by family members, as in Jowai and Cherapunjee, Meghalaya; declared illegal by the National Green Tribunal.
Ferrous mineralA mineral containing iron — iron ore and manganese; they account for about three-fourths of the value of metallic mineral production.
Non-ferrous mineralA mineral not containing iron — copper, bauxite, lead, zinc and gold.
MagnetiteThe finest iron ore, with iron content up to 70 per cent and excellent magnetic qualities, valuable in the electrical industry.
HematiteThe most important industrial iron ore in terms of quantity used, with 50–60 per cent iron content.
Ferro-manganese alloyAn alloy of iron and manganese; nearly 10 kg of manganese is needed for one tonne of steel.
BauxiteA clay-like substance from which alumina and later aluminium is obtained; formed by decomposition of rocks rich in aluminium silicates.
MicaA mineral made of plates or leaves that split into thin sheets; valued for di-electric strength, low power loss, insulation and resistance to high voltage.
LimestoneA rock mineral of calcium carbonate (or calcium and magnesium carbonates); the basic raw material for cement and essential for smelting iron ore.
Conventional energyEnergy from firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity (hydel and thermal).
Non-conventional energyRenewable energy from solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and atomic sources.
PeatCoal formed from decaying plants in swamps; low carbon, high moisture and low heating capacity.
LigniteLow grade brown coal, soft with high moisture content; principal reserves at Neyveli, Tamil Nadu.
Bituminous coalCoal buried deep and subjected to increased temperature; the most popular coal in commercial use.
AnthraciteThe highest quality hard coal.
Metallurgical coalHigh grade bituminous coal with special value for smelting iron in blast furnaces.
Gondwana coalCoal of rock series a little over 200 million years old, found mainly in the Damodar valley (West Bengal–Jharkhand).
Tertiary coalCoal about 55 million years old, found in Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland.
Nodal industryAn industry on which several others depend — petroleum refineries are the nodal industry for synthetic textiles, fertiliser and chemical industries.
CNG and PNGCompressed natural gas, used as a transport fuel, and piped natural gas, used as a cooking fuel at home.
Photovoltaic technologyTechnology that converts sunlight directly into electricity.
Gobar gas plantA biogas plant using cattle dung, giving the farmer energy and improved manure.
Geothermal energyHeat and electricity produced from the heat of the earth’s interior; India has experimental projects at Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh) and Puga Valley (Ladakh).
05

Important Dates, Facts, Figures and Examples

Everything worth remembering

Numbers and figures

  • Over 2,000 minerals identified; workable deposits are about 1 per cent of the earth’s crust.
  • Mineral intake is about 0.3 per cent of total nutrient intake, yet enables use of the other 99.7 per cent.
  • Three-fourths of the value of metallic mineral production comes from ferrous minerals.
  • Magnetite: up to 70 per cent iron; hematite: 50–60 per cent.
  • 97 per cent of iron ore production (2018–19) from Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Jharkhand.
  • Bailadila range: 14 deposits of super high grade hematite.
  • 10 kg of manganese per tonne of steel.
  • Odisha produced 65 per cent of India’s bauxite in 2018–19; Madhya Pradesh 33 per cent of manganese.
  • More than 70 per cent of rural household energy from firewood and cattle dung cake.
  • Gondwana coal 200 million years old; tertiary coal 55 million years old.
  • HVJ pipeline 1,700 km; gas pipelines now 18,500 km, heading to over 34,000 km.

07

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

Can you list a number of items used in your house made of metals? Where do these metals come from?

Model answer

Utensils, taps, door handles, locks, almirah, fan, bicycle, wires, nails, scissors and the gas stove are made of metals. Metals are extracted from minerals embedded in the earth’s crust — for example iron from iron ore, aluminium from bauxite and copper from copper ore — after proper refinement.

2.

Find out where these minerals are found (the minerals used in toothpaste).

Model answer

Silica, limestone, aluminium oxide and phosphate minerals are abrasives; fluoride comes from the mineral fluorite; titanium oxide comes from rutile, ilmenite and anatase; the sparkle comes from mica; and the tube and brush are plastics from petroleum. In India, limestone is widespread, mica comes from the Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand, Ajmer in Rajasthan and Nellore in Andhra Pradesh, and bauxite (for aluminium oxide) from the Amarkantak plateau and Odisha’s Panchpatmali.

3.

Dig a little deeper — how many minerals are used to make a light bulb?

Model answer

At least five or six: silica sand (glass bulb), tungsten (filament), aluminium or tin (cap/base), copper or brass (screw base contacts), argon or nitrogen (inert gas filling) and mica or ceramic (insulation). (Answers may vary slightly; the point is that even a simple object needs many minerals.)

4.

Dig a little deeper — what is the difference between an open pit mine, a quarry and an underground mine with shafts?

Model answer

An open pit mine is a large surface excavation for ore that lies near the surface, worked in benches. A quarry is a surface working for stone, sand or limestone, usually shallower and for building material. An underground mine with shafts is used where the ore lies deep: vertical shafts are sunk and horizontal galleries follow the seam or vein, as in coal mining.

5.

Why does a mineral “deposit” or “reserve” become a mine only sometimes?

Model answer

Because the concentration of the mineral in the ore, the ease of extraction and the closeness to the market decide whether extraction is economically viable. Only when a choice is made to extract — because these conditions are favourable — does a deposit or reserve turn into a mine.

6.

Dig a little deeper — superimpose the maps of iron ore, manganese, coal and the iron and steel industry. Do you see any correlation? Why?

Model answer

Yes. Iron and steel plants are concentrated on the Chota Nagpur plateau and in Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Jharkhand, where iron ore, manganese and coal occur close together. Steel needs iron ore, coking coal and limestone in the ratio of about 4:2:1 plus some manganese, and all these raw materials are heavy and bulky, so plants locate near them.

7.

Dig a little deeper — locate the mines of bauxite on the physical map of India.

Model answer

Bauxite is found mainly in the Amarkantak plateau, the Maikal hills and the Bilaspur–Katni plateau region, with the most important deposits at Panchpatmali in Koraput district, Odisha — that is, across the Chota Nagpur and central Indian plateau belt.

8.

Dig a little deeper — why is Chota Nagpur a storehouse of minerals?

Model answer

Because the region is part of the ancient, stable peninsular rock system, rich in metallic minerals, coal and mica. Long geological time, igneous intrusions that formed veins and lodes, and metamorphism concentrated iron ore, manganese, bauxite, mica and coal in this plateau.

9.

Dig a little deeper — make a list of items where substitutes are used instead of minerals. Where are these substitutes obtained from?

Model answer

Plastic pipes instead of metal; aluminium instead of copper in wiring; glass, ceramic and plastic instead of metals in containers; recycled scrap metal in place of fresh ore; and biomass, solar and wind energy in place of coal and oil. Substitutes come from petrochemicals, clay and sand, recycled waste and renewable natural flows.

10.

Name some river valley projects and write the names of the dams built on these rivers.

Model answer

Bhakra–Nangal on the Sutlej; Hirakud on the Mahanadi; Damodar Valley Corporation projects on the Damodar; Kopili Hydel Project in Assam; Sardar Sarovar on the Narmada; Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna.

11.

Locate the six nuclear power stations and find out the state in which they are located.

Model answer

Read the map “Distribution of Nuclear and Thermal Power Plants” (Map 5.3). India’s nuclear power stations are at Tarapur (Maharashtra), Rawatbhata (Rajasthan), Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu), Narora (Uttar Pradesh), Kakrapar (Gujarat) and Kaiga (Karnataka). The chapter itself only names Rawat Bhata on the map.

12.

Collect information about cross-country natural gas pipelines laid by GAIL under “One Nation One Grid”.

Model answer

The first was the 1,700 km Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur (HVJ) pipeline linking Mumbai High and Bassein fields to fertiliser, power and industrial complexes in western and northern India. India’s cross-country gas pipeline network has grown from 1,700 km to 18,500 km and is expected to cross 34,000 km as a Gas Grid linking all gas sources and consuming markets, including the North-Eastern states.

08

NCERT Exercise Questions and Answers

End-of-chapter exercises, projects and activities

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following minerals is formed by decomposition of rocks, leaving a residual mass of weathered material? (a) coal (b) bauxite (c) gold (d) zinc

Model answer

(b) Bauxite. It is formed by the decomposition of surface rocks and the removal of soluble constituents, leaving a residual mass of weathered material containing ores.

2.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Koderma, in Jharkhand, is the leading producer of which one of the following minerals? (a) bauxite (b) mica (c) iron ore (d) copper

Model answer

(b) Mica. The Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand is the leading producer of mica.

3.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Minerals are deposited and accumulated in the strata of which of the following rocks? (a) sedimentary rocks (b) metamorphic rocks (c) igneous rocks (d) none of the above

Model answer

(a) Sedimentary rocks. Minerals occur there in beds or layers, formed by deposition, accumulation and concentration in horizontal strata.

4.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following minerals is contained in the Monazite sand? (a) oil (b) uranium (c) thorium (d) coal

Model answer

(c) Thorium. The monazite sands of Kerala are rich in thorium.

5.
NCERT exercise2 marks

Distinguish between ferrous and non-ferrous minerals. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Ferrous minerals contain iron — iron ore and manganese — and account for about three-fourths of the value of metallic mineral production. Non-ferrous minerals do not contain iron — copper, bauxite, lead, zinc and gold.

6.
NCERT exercise2 marks

Distinguish between conventional and non-conventional sources of energy. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Conventional sources are firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity (hydel and thermal), mostly non-renewable and polluting. Non-conventional sources are solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and atomic energy — renewable and cleaner.

7.
NCERT exercise2 marks

What is a mineral? (about 30 words)

Model answer

A mineral is a homogenous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure. Minerals range from the hardest diamond to the softest talc, and are classified by geologists using colour, hardness, crystal form, lustre and density.

8.
NCERT exercise2 marks

How are minerals formed in igneous and metamorphic rocks? (about 30 words)

Model answer

In igneous and metamorphic rocks, minerals occur in cracks, crevices, faults or joints — the smaller occurrences are veins and the larger are lodes. They form when minerals in liquid, molten and gaseous forms are forced upward through cavities and cool and solidify as they rise.

9.
NCERT exercise2 marks

Why do we need to conserve mineral resources? (about 30 words)

Model answer

Because workable mineral deposits are only about one per cent of the earth’s crust and were formed over millions of years; mineral resources are finite and non-renewable, and continued extraction from greater depths raises costs while quality falls.

10.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Describe the distribution of coal in India. (about 120 words)

Model answer

Coal in India occurs in rock series of two main geological ages. Gondwana coal, a little over 200 million years old and mostly metallurgical coal, is located in the Damodar valley (West Bengal–Jharkhand), where Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro are important coalfields; the Godavari, Mahanadi, Son and Wardha valleys also contain coal deposits. Tertiary coal, only about 55 million years old, occurs in the north-eastern states of Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland. Lignite, a low grade brown coal, has its principal reserves at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu and is used for generating electricity. Because coal is bulky and loses weight on use as it is reduced to ash, heavy industries and thermal power stations are located on or near the coalfields. India is highly dependent on coal, its most abundantly available fossil fuel, for commercial energy requirements.

11.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Why do you think that solar energy has a bright future in India? (about 120 words)

Model answer

India is a tropical country with abundant sunshine for most of the year, so it has enormous possibilities of tapping solar energy. Photovoltaic technology converts sunlight directly into electricity, and solar energy is already becoming popular in rural and remote areas where grid supply is unreliable. Big solar power plants are being established in different parts of India, which will reduce the dependence of rural households on firewood and dung cakes — in turn contributing to environmental conservation and to adequate supply of manure for agriculture, since dung will no longer be burnt. Solar energy is renewable and clean, and it helps meet the twin planks of sustainable energy: energy conservation and increased use of renewable sources. It also reduces the import burden of fossil fuels, whose prices are rising and whose supply is uncertain.

12.
NCERT activityActivity

Activity — Fill in the names of the correct minerals in the crossword. DOWN: (1) Found in placer deposit (4); (2) Iron ore mined in Bailadila (8); (3) Indispensable for the electrical industry (4); (4) Geological age of coal found in north-east India (8); (5) Formed in veins and lodes (3). ACROSS: (1) A ferrous mineral (9); (2) Raw material for the cement industry (9); (3) Finest iron ore with magnetic properties (9); (4) Highest quality hard coal (10); (5) Aluminium is obtained from this ore (7); (6) Khetri mines are famous for this mineral (6); (7) Formed due to evaporation (6).

Model answer

Down: (1) GOLD (2) HEMATITE (3) MICA (4) TERTIARY (5) TIN.
Across: (1) MANGANESE (2) LIMESTONE (3) MAGNETITE (4) ANTHRACITE (5) BAUXITE (6) COPPER (7) GYPSUM.

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

Explain the modes of occurrence of minerals with examples. (5 marks)

Model answer

(i) In igneous and metamorphic rocks, in cracks, crevices, faults or joints — smaller occurrences are veins and larger ones are lodes; tin, copper, zinc and lead come from these. (ii) In sedimentary rocks, in beds or layers formed by deposition and concentration in horizontal strata — coal, some iron ore, and gypsum, potash salt and sodium salt formed by evaporation. (iii) By decomposition of surface rocks and removal of soluble constituents, leaving a residual mass — bauxite. (iv) As placer deposits in the sands of valley floors and the base of hills — gold, silver, tin, platinum. (v) In ocean waters and on ocean beds — common salt, magnesium, bromine and manganese nodules.

2.

Describe the four major iron ore belts of India. (5 marks)

Model answer

Odisha–Jharkhand: high grade hematite in Badampahar mines (Mayurbhanj and Kendujhar) and in Gua and Noamundi in Singhbhum, Jharkhand. Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur: very high grade hematite in the Bailadila range of Bastar, Chhattisgarh, with 14 deposits having the best physical properties for steel making; exported to Japan and South Korea via Vishakhapatnam port. Ballari–Chitradurga–Chikkamagaluru–Tumakuru: large reserves in Karnataka, with Kudremukh mines in the Western Ghats, a 100 per cent export unit, ore transported as slurry through a pipeline to a port near Mangaluru. Maharashtra–Goa: Goa and Ratnagiri district of Maharashtra; ores not of very high quality but efficiently exploited, exported through Marmagao port.

3.

Distinguish between magnetite and hematite. (2 marks)

Model answer

Magnetite is the finest iron ore with iron content up to 70 per cent and excellent magnetic qualities, especially valuable in the electrical industry. Hematite is the most important industrial iron ore in terms of the quantity used, but has a slightly lower iron content of 50–60 per cent.

4.

Why is India’s production of non-ferrous minerals unsatisfactory? Describe copper and bauxite. (5 marks)

Model answer

The chapter says India’s reserves and production of non-ferrous minerals is not very satisfactory, although copper, bauxite, lead, zinc and gold play a vital role in metallurgical, engineering and electrical industries. Copper: India is critically deficient in reserve and production; being malleable, ductile and a good conductor, copper is used in electrical cables, electronics and chemical industries, and the Balaghat mines (Madhya Pradesh), Khetri mines (Rajasthan) and Singhbhum district (Jharkhand) are leading producers. Bauxite: a clay-like substance from which alumina and later aluminium is obtained; deposits form by decomposition of rocks rich in aluminium silicates and are found in the Amarkantak plateau, Maikal hills and Bilaspur–Katni plateau. Odisha was the largest producer in 2018–19, with Panchpatmali deposits in Koraput district the most important.

5.

Why is mica indispensable in the electrical and electronic industries? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because of its excellent di-electric strength, low power loss factor, insulating properties and resistance to high voltage. Mica is made up of plates or leaves that split into very thin sheets, and it is found in the northern edge of the Chota Nagpur plateau — the Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand is the leading producer, with Ajmer in Rajasthan and the Nellore belt of Andhra Pradesh also important.

6.

Explain the hazards of mining. (3 marks)

Model answer

The dust and noxious fumes inhaled by miners make them vulnerable to pulmonary diseases; the risk of collapsing mine roofs, inundation and fires in coalmines is a constant threat; water sources in the region get contaminated; and dumping of waste and slurry degrades land and soil and increases stream and river pollution. Stricter safety regulations and implementation of environmental laws are essential to prevent mining from becoming a “killer industry”.

7.

Why must mineral resources be conserved, and how? (5 marks)

Model answer

Workable mineral deposits are an insignificant fraction — one per cent — of the earth’s crust, and mineral formation is so slow that rates of replenishment are infinitely small compared with consumption. Mineral resources are therefore finite and non-renewable, and continued extraction from greater depths raises costs while quality falls. Conservation requires planned and sustainable use: constantly evolving improved technologies to allow the use of low grade ores at low costs, recycling of metals, using scrap metals, and using other substitutes.

8.

Distinguish between conventional and non-conventional energy sources with examples. (3 marks)

Model answer

Conventional sources include firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity (hydel and thermal) — most are non-renewable and polluting, and more than 70 per cent of rural household energy comes from firewood and dung cake. Non-conventional sources include solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and atomic energy — renewable and cleaner, and India has the largest programmes for their development.

9.

Describe the formation and forms of coal. (5 marks)

Model answer

Coal is formed due to the compression of plant material over millions of years, and occurs in forms depending on the degree of compression and the depth and time of burial. Peat is produced by decaying plants in swamps, with low carbon, high moisture and low heating capacity. Lignite is a low grade brown coal, soft and with high moisture content; principal reserves are at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu, used for electricity. Bituminous coal is buried deep and subjected to increased temperatures and is the most popular coal in commercial use. Anthracite is the highest quality hard coal. Metallurgical coal is high grade bituminous coal with special value for smelting iron in blast furnaces.

10.

How does petroleum occur, and where is it found in India? (5 marks)

Model answer

Most petroleum occurrences in India are associated with anticlines and fault traps in rock formations of the tertiary age. In regions of folding, oil occurs where it is trapped in the crest of the upfold; the oil-bearing layer is a porous limestone or sandstone through which oil may flow, and the oil is prevented from rising or sinking by intervening non-porous layers. Petroleum is also found in fault traps between porous and non-porous rocks, and gas, being lighter, usually occurs above the oil. Mumbai High, Gujarat and Assam are the major production areas; Ankeleshwar is the most important field of Gujarat and Assam is the oldest oil producing state, with Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran-Hugrijan as important fields. Petroleum refineries act as a nodal industry for synthetic textile, fertiliser and chemical industries.

11.

Explain hydro and thermal electricity. (3 marks)

Model answer

Electricity is generated mainly in two ways. Hydro electricity is generated by fast flowing water, which drives hydro turbines; water is a renewable resource, and India has multi-purpose projects such as Bhakra Nangal, the Damodar Valley Corporation and the Kopili Hydel Project. Thermal electricity is generated by burning coal, petroleum and natural gas to drive turbines, using non-renewable fossil fuels. Once generated, the electricity is exactly the same, and per capita consumption is considered an index of development.

12.

Describe nuclear, solar and wind energy in India. (5 marks)

Model answer

Nuclear energy is obtained by altering the structure of atoms, releasing heat that generates electric power; uranium and thorium are available in Jharkhand and the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan, and the monazite sands of Kerala are rich in thorium. Solar energy is tapped through photovoltaic technology that converts sunlight directly into electricity; India, a tropical country, has enormous possibilities, and solar energy is becoming popular in rural and remote areas, reducing dependence on firewood and dung cakes. Wind power: India has great potential, and the largest wind farm cluster is in Tamil Nadu from Nagarcoil to Madurai, with important farms in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Gujarat, Kerala, Maharashtra and Lakshadweep; Nagarcoil and Jaisalmer are well known for effective use of wind energy.

13.

Describe biogas, tidal and geothermal energy. (5 marks)

Model answer

Biogas: shrubs, farm waste and animal and human waste are decomposed to yield gas with higher thermal efficiency than kerosene, dung cake and charcoal; plants are set up at municipal, cooperative and individual levels, and those using cattle dung are called gobar gas plants, giving the farmer energy and improved manure. Tidal energy: floodgate dams are built across inlets; water trapped at high tide flows back through a pipe carrying a turbine. The Gulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kuchchh in Gujarat and the Gangetic delta in the Sunderbans provide ideal conditions. Geothermal energy: heat from the earth’s interior; where the geothermal gradient is high, groundwater turns to steam that drives turbines. Two experimental projects exist — Parvati valley near Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh) and Puga Valley (Ladakh).

14.

Why is energy conservation called a source of energy? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because saving energy avoids the need to generate it. India is one of the least energy efficient countries in the world, and energy consumption is rising in every sector. Promotion of energy conservation and increased use of renewable sources are the twin planks of sustainable energy, and as citizens we can use public transport, switch off electricity when not in use and use power-saving devices — hence the chapter’s statement that “energy saved is energy produced”.

10

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Asked in CBSE board exams

Previous year questions

These follow the pattern of questions set in CBSE Social Science papers for this chapter. Answers are model answers.

1.
CBSE pattern

Why are heavy industries and thermal power stations located near coalfields? (CBSE pattern, 2 marks)

Model answer

Because coal is a bulky material which loses weight on use as it is reduced to ash, so transporting it is costly. Locating near the coalfield reduces transport cost.

2.
CBSE pattern

Name the two types of iron ore found in India with their iron content. (2 marks)

Model answer

Magnetite, with up to 70 per cent iron and excellent magnetic qualities; and hematite, the most important industrial iron ore in quantity used, with 50–60 per cent iron.

3.
CBSE pattern

Which state is the largest producer of bauxite and which deposits are most important? (2 marks)

Model answer

Odisha was the largest bauxite producing state in 2018–19, and the Panchpatmali deposits in Koraput district are the most important in the state.

4.
CBSE pattern

Why are petroleum refineries called a “nodal industry”? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because they provide raw materials to synthetic textile, fertiliser and numerous chemical industries, on which those industries depend.

5.
CBSE pattern

What is rat-hole mining and why has it been declared illegal? (3 marks)

Model answer

In Meghalaya, where coal, iron ore, limestone and dolomite are owned by individuals or communities, coal mining in Jowai and Cherapunjee is done by family members in the form of a long narrow tunnel — “rat-hole” mining. The National Green Tribunal has declared such activities illegal and recommended they be stopped forthwith, because of the danger to life and the damage to the environment.

6.
CBSE pattern

What are placer deposits? Name two minerals found in them. (2 marks)

Model answer

Alluvial deposits in the sands of valley floors and the base of hills, containing minerals that are not corroded by water. Gold, silver, tin and platinum are the most important.

7.
CBSE pattern

Explain the significance of the HVJ pipeline. (3 marks)

Model answer

The 1,700 km Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur cross-country gas pipeline, built by GAIL (India), linked the Mumbai High and Bassein gas fields with fertiliser, power and industrial complexes in western and northern India. It provided impetus to Indian gas market development; the network has since expanded to 18,500 km and is expected to cross 34,000 km as a Gas Grid.

8.
CBSE pattern

Where are India’s geothermal energy projects located? (2 marks)

Model answer

One in the Parvati valley near Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh, and the other in the Puga Valley, Ladakh.

9.
CBSE pattern

What are the twin planks of sustainable energy? (2 marks)

Model answer

Promotion of energy conservation and increased use of renewable energy sources.

10.
CBSE pattern

Name the minerals used in the electrical industry and say where they are found. (3 marks)

Model answer

Mica — Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand, Ajmer in Rajasthan and Nellore in Andhra Pradesh; copper — Balaghat (Madhya Pradesh), Khetri (Rajasthan), Singhbhum (Jharkhand); and magnetite, valued for its magnetic qualities, from the iron ore belts.

11

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Is a mineral the same as a rock?

Model answer

No. A mineral is a homogenous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure. A rock is a combination of such minerals — some rocks, like limestone, consist of a single mineral, but most contain several.

2.

Which is the finest iron ore?

Model answer

Magnetite, with iron content up to 70 per cent and excellent magnetic qualities.

3.

Why is India called critically deficient in copper?

Model answer

Because its reserves and production of copper are not satisfactory, even though copper is essential for electrical cables, electronics and chemical industries.

4.

Which coal is best for smelting iron?

Model answer

Metallurgical coal — high grade bituminous coal with special value for smelting iron in blast furnaces.

5.

Why is dung cake use being discouraged?

Model answer

Because it consumes the most valuable manure which could be used in agriculture; biogas is a more efficient use of cattle dung.

6.

Where are the largest wind farms in India?

Model answer

The largest wind farm cluster is in Tamil Nadu, from Nagarcoil to Madurai; Nagarcoil and Jaisalmer are well known for effective use of wind energy.

7.

Is atomic energy a conventional or non-conventional source?

Model answer

Non-conventional — the chapter lists atomic energy with solar, wind, tidal, geothermal and biogas.

8.

Why are minerals called non-renewable?

Model answer

Because they took millions of years to form and the rate of replenishment is infinitely small compared with consumption; workable deposits are only about one per cent of the earth’s crust.

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): Minerals are an indispensable part of our lives.
Reason (R): Almost everything we use, from a pin to a ship, is made from minerals.

2.

Assertion (A): Bauxite is formed by the decomposition of surface rocks.
Reason (R): Soluble constituents are removed, leaving a residual mass of weathered material containing ore.

3.

Assertion (A): Magnetite is the finest iron ore.
Reason (R): Hematite has a higher iron content than magnetite.

4.

Assertion (A): India is self-sufficient in copper.
Reason (R): Copper is used in electrical cables, electronics and chemical industries.

5.

Assertion (A): Mica is used in electric and electronic industries.
Reason (R): It has excellent di-electric strength, low power loss factor and resistance to high voltage.

6.

Assertion (A): Heavy industries and thermal power stations are located near coalfields.
Reason (R): Coal is a bulky material that loses weight on use as it is reduced to ash.

7.

Assertion (A): Petroleum refineries are called a nodal industry.
Reason (R): They provide raw material to synthetic textile, fertiliser and chemical industries.

8.

Assertion (A): Coal is a renewable resource.
Reason (R): Coal is formed by the compression of plant material over millions of years.

9.

Assertion (A): Biogas is the most efficient use of cattle dung.
Reason (R): It improves the quality of manure and prevents the loss of trees and manure due to burning.

10.

Assertion (A): Energy conservation is called a source of energy.
Reason (R): Energy saved is energy produced.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — A bright smile from toothpaste and minerals

Source extract

Toothpaste cleans your teeth. Abrasive minerals like silica, limestone, aluminium oxide and various phosphate minerals do the cleaning. Fluoride which is used to reduce cavities comes from a mineral fluorite. Most toothpaste is made white with titanium oxide, which comes from minerals called rutile, ilmenite and anatase. The sparkle in some toothpastes comes from mica. The toothbrush and the tube containing the paste are made of plastics from petroleum.

1.

Name three abrasive minerals used in toothpaste.

Model answer

Silica, limestone and aluminium oxide (also various phosphate minerals).

2.

Which mineral provides fluoride, and which three minerals give the white colour?

Model answer

Fluoride comes from fluorite; whiteness comes from titanium oxide obtained from rutile, ilmenite and anatase.

3.

What does this passage show about the importance of minerals?

Model answer

That minerals are indispensable in everyday life: even a simple tube of toothpaste depends on several minerals, and the tube itself is made of plastics from petroleum.

Source 2 — Rat-hole mining in Meghalaya

Case study

Most of the minerals in India are nationalised and their extraction is possible only after obtaining due permission from the government. But in most of the tribal areas of north-east India, minerals are owned by individuals or communities. In Meghalaya there are large deposits of coal, iron ore, limestone and dolomite. Coal mining in Jowai and Cherapunjee is done by family members in the form of a long narrow tunnel, known as “rat-hole” mining. The National Green Tribunal has declared such activities illegal and recommended that these should be stopped forthwith.

1.

How does mineral ownership in north-east India differ from the rest of the country?

Model answer

Elsewhere minerals are nationalised and extraction needs government permission; in most tribal areas of the north-east, minerals are owned by individuals or communities.

2.

Why is this mining method called “rat-hole” mining?

Model answer

Because coal is extracted through a long narrow tunnel, like a rat hole, dug by family members.

3.

What has the National Green Tribunal said about it?

Model answer

That such activities are illegal and should be stopped forthwith.

Which state dominates bauxite production and by how much?

2.

3.

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

Why do so many mineral-based industries cluster on the Chota Nagpur plateau? Use the chapter’s logic of location.

Model answer

Because iron ore, manganese, coal, bauxite, mica and limestone occur close together in the ancient peninsular rock system, and the concentration of mineral in the ore, ease of extraction and closeness to the market decide economic viability. Heavy, bulky raw materials are costly to move, so industries locate near them — the same reason heavy industries and thermal plants sit on coalfields. (Model answer.)

2.

“Minerals are a one-time gift.” Explain, and suggest how a country should use them.

Model answer

Workable deposits are only about one per cent of the earth’s crust and were formed over millions of years; the rate of replenishment is infinitely small compared with consumption, so minerals are finite and non-renewable. A country should use them in a planned and sustainable way: evolve technologies for low grade ores, recycle metals, use scrap and substitutes, avoid wasteful extraction and export of raw ore, and invest the returns in renewable energy and human capital. (Model answer.)

3.

Compare coal and solar energy as the basis of India’s future energy supply.

Model answer

Coal is India’s most abundantly available fossil fuel and is used for power generation, industry and domestic needs, but it is non-renewable, bulky, polluting and costly to transport, which is why plants sit on coalfields. Solar is renewable and clean, uses photovoltaic technology, suits rural and remote areas, and reduces dependence on firewood and dung — but it needs land, storage and investment. The chapter’s “twin planks of sustainable energy” — conservation plus more renewable use — suggest a transition rather than an overnight switch. (Model answer.)

4.

Why is aluminium called a metal of the future, and why did its value change so dramatically?

Model answer

Because it combines the strength of metals such as iron with extreme lightness, good conductivity and great malleability, so it substitutes for steel, copper, zinc and lead in many industries. The Napoleon box shows how value depends on technology: when extraction was difficult, aluminium was fit for an emperor; thirty years later, with better technology, aluminium bowls were common with beggars in Paris. (Model answer.)

5.

A village has cattle, farm waste, plenty of sun and a hill stream. Design an energy plan for it using this chapter.

Model answer

(i) A gobar gas (biogas) plant using cattle dung and farm waste — giving cooking gas and better manure, and ending the burning of dung cakes and fuel wood. (ii) Solar photovoltaic panels or a solar pump for lighting and irrigation. (iii) A micro-hydro unit on the hill stream if the flow and fall are adequate, as with hydel projects. (iv) Improved chulhas and power-saving devices to conserve energy. Together these replace firewood, protect the forest and improve health. (Model answer.)

6.

Mining gives us everything from pins to ships, yet the chapter calls it a potential “killer industry”. How can both be true?

Model answer

Both are true because the benefits are enjoyed widely while the costs fall on miners and nearby communities: pulmonary diseases from dust and fumes, collapsing roofs, inundation and fires, contaminated water, and land and river pollution from dumped waste and slurry. The remedy is not to stop mining but to enforce stricter safety regulations and environmental laws, rehabilitate mined land and involve local people in decisions. (Model answer.)

Quick Revision Sheet

One page before the exam

Minerals — basics

  • Mineral: homogenous, naturally occurring, definable internal structure; over 2,000 identified.
  • Geographer: distribution and economic activities; geologist: formation, age, composition.
  • Classification: metallic (ferrous, non-ferrous, precious), non-metallic, energy minerals.

Occurrence

  • Igneous/metamorphic: veins and lodes (tin, copper, zinc, lead).
  • Sedimentary: beds and layers (coal, iron ore, gypsum, potash salt, sodium salt).
  • Residual mass after decomposition: bauxite.
  • Placer deposits: gold, silver, tin, platinum.
  • Ocean: common salt, magnesium, bromine; manganese nodules.
  • Rat-hole mining — Meghalaya; NGT declared it illegal.

Ferrous

  • Three-fourths of metallic mineral value.
  • Magnetite 70% iron, magnetic; hematite 50–60%, most used.
  • 97% of output from Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Jharkhand (2018–19).
  • Belts: Odisha–Jharkhand; Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur (Bailadila, 14 deposits, Vishakhapatnam); Ballari–Chitradurga–Chikkamagaluru–Tumakuru (Kudremukh, slurry to Mangaluru); Maharashtra–Goa (Marmagao).
  • Manganese: 10 kg per tonne of steel; MP 33%, Maharashtra 27%, Odisha 16%.

Non-ferrous, non-metallic, rock

  • Copper: deficient; Balaghat, Khetri, Singhbhum; cables, electronics.
  • Bauxite: Amarkantak, Maikal, Bilaspur–Katni; Odisha 65%, Panchpatmali.
  • Mica: plates/leaves, di-electric, Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh, Ajmer, Nellore.
  • Limestone: cement and smelting iron.

Hazards and conservation

  • Pulmonary diseases, roof collapse, inundation, fires, contaminated water, waste dumping.
  • 1% of crust workable; finite, non-renewable; recycle, use scrap, substitutes, better technology.

Energy

  • Conventional: firewood, dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas, electricity (hydel, thermal).
  • Non-conventional: nuclear, solar, wind, biogas, tidal, geothermal.
  • >70% of rural household energy from firewood and dung cake.

Coal, oil, gas

  • Peat, lignite (Neyveli), bituminous, anthracite; metallurgical coal.
  • Gondwana (200 my) Damodar valley: Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro; also Godavari, Mahanadi, Son, Wardha.
  • Tertiary (55 my): Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland.
  • Petroleum: anticlines and fault traps; Mumbai High, Ankeleshwar, Digboi, Naharkatiya, Moran-Hugrijan; nodal industry.
  • Gas: HVJ 1,700 km → 18,500 km → 34,000 km Gas Grid; CNG, PNG; Krishna–Godavari.

Non-conventional details

  • Nuclear: uranium and thorium — Jharkhand, Aravalli (Rajasthan); monazite sands of Kerala.
  • Solar: photovoltaic; Wind: Nagarcoil–Madurai, Jaisalmer.
  • Biogas: gobar gas plants; Tidal: Khambhat, Kuchchh, Sunderbans.
  • Geothermal: Manikaran (HP), Puga Valley (Ladakh).
  • “Energy saved is energy produced.”

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

Minerals are an indispensable part of our lives — everything from a pin to a ship is made from them, and even our food contains them. A mineral is a homogenous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure; an ore is an accumulation of a mineral mixed with other elements in a concentration that makes extraction commercially viable. Minerals occur in veins and lodes in igneous and metamorphic rocks, in beds and layers in sedimentary rocks, as residual masses after decomposition (bauxite), as placer deposits (gold, silver, tin, platinum) and in ocean waters and beds.

India’s minerals are unevenly distributed: the peninsular rocks hold most coal, metallic and non-metallic minerals, sedimentary rocks of Gujarat and Assam hold petroleum, Rajasthan has non-ferrous minerals, and the northern alluvial plains are almost devoid of economic minerals. Ferrous minerals — iron ore (magnetite and hematite) and manganese — account for about three-fourths of the value of metallic mineral production, with four major iron ore belts and exports through Vishakhapatnam, Marmagao and a port near Mangaluru. Non-ferrous minerals include copper (in which India is critically deficient) and bauxite; mica and limestone are the important non-metallic and rock minerals. Mining brings hazards — disease, collapse, contaminated water and pollution — and minerals, being only one per cent of the crust and non-renewable, must be conserved through better technology, recycling and substitutes.

Energy resources are conventional (firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas, hydel and thermal electricity) and non-conventional (nuclear, solar, wind, biogas, tidal and geothermal). Coal occurs as peat, lignite, bituminous and anthracite, in Gondwana and tertiary deposits; petroleum is trapped in anticlines and fault traps and refineries act as a nodal industry; natural gas is increasingly used as CNG and PNG, carried by the HVJ and a growing gas grid. India’s energy future rests on the twin planks of conservation and renewable energy — “energy saved is energy produced”.
